Polynomial function. An algebraic function whose definition is a sum of terms, each a constant coefficient times a variable raised to a non-negative integer power. Polynomials are the most fundamental class of functions in mathematics. They are continuous and differentiable everywhere, with explicit formulas for roots up to degree four, and appear ubiquitously in physics, engineering, and economics as models of real phenomena. Their structure—degree, roots, end behaviour—is central to calculus and forms the foundation for understanding more complex functions.

A polynomial is expressed in standard form as a n times x to the n, plus a n minus one times x to the n minus one, plus continuing down to a one times x plus a zero, where the exponents are non-negative integers, the coefficients a i are real or complex, and a n is not zero. The degree is the highest power of x that appears. It determines fundamental behaviour: the number of roots, turning points, and end behaviour. Degree zero is constant, degree one is linear, degree two is quadratic, degree three is cubic, degree four is quartic, and degree five and higher are quintic, sextic, septic, and so on. The coefficients determine the polynomial's specific shape and roots.

Polynomials are continuous and differentiable everywhere on the real line, in fact, infinitely differentiable. They are one of the smoothest function classes. The derivative of a n times x to the n plus continuing to a zero is n times a n times x to the n minus one plus continuing to a one. The derivative is a polynomial of degree n minus one. Integrating a polynomial yields another polynomial plus a constant. Every polynomial is its own Taylor series since its expansion is finite.

The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra guarantees that a degree-n polynomial has exactly n roots in the complex numbers, counting multiplicity. It may have fewer real roots. The Rational Root Theorem says if a polynomial has integer coefficients and a rational root p divided by q in lowest terms, then p divides the constant term and q divides the leading coefficient. A degree-n polynomial factors uniquely into n linear factors: f of x equals a n times the product of x minus r i for each root r i. A root may appear more than once, such as x minus two squared, which has a double root at x equals two. This multiplicity affects the shape of the graph.

End behaviour is determined by the leading term a n times x to the n. If n is even and a n is positive, then f of x approaches positive infinity as x approaches positive or negative infinity. If n is odd and a n is positive, then f of x approaches negative infinity as x approaches negative infinity and positive infinity as x approaches positive infinity. A degree-n polynomial has at most n minus one turning points, local extrema found where f prime of x equals zero. It has at most n minus two inflection points where concavity changes.

Polynomials are the gateway to both theoretical and applied mathematics. Theoretically, they motivated the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, the theory of fields and rings, and Galois theory of equations. Practically, they model countless phenomena: projectile motion, population growth, economic cost functions, signal processing, and numerical methods.
